title: RANCOR IN THE RANKS: Toronto Police under the gun in 2019
article: In the wake of a tumultuous year marred by unprecedented violence and growing frustration among the city's frontline cops, the Toronto Police Service faces some difficult issues in 2019.

Some of those issues - such as short staffing and declining morale - will likely come to a head in coming months as the Toronto Police Association and Toronto Police Services Board sit down to hammer out a new contract for the 4,800 uniformed officers and 2,500 civilians employed by the service.

"Morale is lower than it's ever been...our members are fed up," TPA President Mike McCormack told the Sun recently, explaining his members' contract expired at the end of 2018 and negotiations for a new deal are set to begin this month.
As cops tried to keep up with radio calls and worked more overtime than they could handle last year, bodies piled up in numbers never before seen in the city.
By the end of 2018, there were a record high 96 murders. And 51 of those victims were killed by guns - one shy of another record high.
"None of our people are surprised by the increased gun violence," McCormack said.
He and others in the policing world have been sounding the alarm bells for several years as shootings in the city spiked dramatically.

But city politicians and TPS senior command insisted the city is safe and made assurances, despite criticism from front line officers, modernization plans including streamlining the service and doing more with less would help address public safety.
As cops found themselves reacting to crime - not always in a timely fashion - and proactive policing fell by the wayside, frustration mounted.

In February, the TPA held a "no confidence" vote on Chief Mark Saunders' leadership. Slightly less than half the membership participated, but 86% of those who voted made it clear they had lost confidence in the city's top cop.
At the time, McCormack complained cost-cutting measures and a reduction of cops on the street was jeopardizing the safety of officers and the city.
He also pointed out increased stress was prompting many officers to retire as soon as they were eligible, join other GTA services or leave the job entirely.
One veteran officer, Const. Stefan Mueller, sent out an email in May to all service members - including top brass - pleading for more cops to be put on the street before someone gets hurt.

And another longtime cop, Sgt. Mark Hayward, emailed a letter on July 5 to Mayor John Tory - as a private citizen using a personal electronic device - criticizing him for the increased gun and gang violence in the city.

"I feel you are a direct contributor to this violence with your stance and support on the cancellation of the TAVIS program ," he wrote. "You flip-flopped on carding and supported its demise. You forced budget and staffing cuts on the Toronto Police."
The day the letter was sent police responded to a call for a man with a gun in a vehicle at a Scarborough pub.
As officers approached, the man opened fire through the vehicle's window and shot a cop in the chest. Luckily, the officer was saved by his bullet proof vest.
Cops returned fire and killed Robert Morfitt, 36, who had a history of violence and was recently released from prison.

That incident followed a violent Canada Day weekend where two men were killed in an Entertainment District shootout, another was gunned down and three wounded in a Kensington Market shooting, and yet another was stabbed to death on the Danforth.

Days later, Tory and Saunders announced their Gun Violence Reduction Strategy - a plan that included putting 200 extra officers on the street for eight weeks, which cost millions of dollars and had no impact on the violence.

As officers were forced to work more overtime, the chief and mayor maintained staffing numbers were not an issue while at the same time pledging to hire 200 new officers by year's end and another 200 in 2019.
A police spokesman said the service hired 234 police constables in 2018.
"Mayor Tory led the charge to hire more officers in 2018 and will continue to push to hire additional officers in 2019," the mayor's spokesman Don Peat said.
The TPA claims only 192 new officers were hired last year.
And McCormack said 295 officers also left the service in 2018 while another 75 are expected to be lost by the end of February.
So by the time the new recruits hit the street they will scarcely put a dent in the officers being lost through attrition.
By the fall of 2018, many cops were becoming increasingly critical of the service's modernization plan, dubbed The Way Forward, with some calling it a step backward.

Not only are gang members freely carrying guns knowing they are unlikely to be stopped by police, but other criminals have also been emboldened by the service's decision not to respond to various non-violent crimes and other incidents.

Police now only respond to collisions if someone is seriously injured, they no longer respond to vehicle break-ins, LCBO and other retail thefts, or security alarms at homes or businesses unless it's verified the thief or burglar is on site.
And in 2018 the mayor announced plans to have bylaw officers respond to noise complaints.
Tory also began pushing for a handgun ban in the city, a move many in the policing world have scoffed at.

In December, the Ontario Human Rights Commission released an interim report on its inquiry into "racial profiling and racial discrimination of Black persons by the Toronto Police Service" that found blacks in the city are nearly 20 times more likely than whites to be shot to death by cops.
McCormack called the report "completely irresponsible" saying it "unfairly condemns the entire service."
"It includes no context and relies on faulty methodology, if any methodology at all," he said.
McCormack said many cops were also upset by the chief's response to the report.

Saunders chose to share a story with media about being racially profiled by mall security rather than defend his officers - perhaps by pointing out the OHRC report reached its conclusion by looking at just 10 fatal police-involved shootings over five years (2013-17) and finding seven of those killed were black, two were white and one was an "other minority."
Interestingly, the only fatal police-involved shooting in Toronto in the last two years was Morfitt, who was white and was killed after opening fire on a cop.

Recently, Justice Michael Tulloch released his report from the Independent Street Checks Review, which found exactly what countless cops have been saying for years - that provincial regulations on police street checks and carding brought in under Kathleen Wynne in 2017 are complicated, created a chill that stopped engagement with the public and "might have encouraged some types of crime to increase."

Although some media have misconstrued the report, McCormack strongly agrees with Tulloch's findings that street checks when utilized properly can be a valuable policing tool, while random carding - the arbitrary collection of information from citizens - has little impact on crime.
While cops were freely conducting street checks and filling out contact cards, murders in Toronto dropped from 80 in 2005 to 51 in 2011.
But frontline cops have told the Sun that under former chief Bill Blair they were pushed to fill out more contact cards, even given quotas, and by 2013 they were carding up to 200,000 people a year.
However, that reportedly included children on their way home from school and senior citizens who called police to report a break-in at their home.
Tulloch has said some cards were even filled out with names and dates from tombstones.
The entire process became tainted and seriously eroded public trust. But then the baby was thrown out with the bathwater and all hell broke loose.
Toronto suspended carding in 2015 and 2016. Police filled out just 25 contact cards in 2017 and shootings jumped to an all-time high.
In the first six months of 2018, cops filled out just one contact card and shootings rose again - up almost 130% from a few years earlier in 2014.

"Justice Tulloch found that street checks are a legitimate and useful policing tool," McCormack said. "But he also said the public needs to be educated on street checks and police officers need better training."

"Hopefully this report doesn't just gather dust because what we need now is a commitment from the chief and the mayor to provide us with resources for training and a proactive policing component," he added.
During the chief's year-end news conference over the holidays, Saunders described 2018 as "a unique year."
"I do think this was a unique year for the loss of life and I don't think that this is going to be a trend that we're going to have every single year," he said.
